REPAIR items/lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval.md: passes only after auto-repair — adopt the canonical form:
  | **Given:** The compact interval $I=[a,b]$, the continuous matrix field $C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$, the time $t_0\in I$, and the initial matrix $Y_0$.
  | 
  | [F1] Picard-Lindelof gives a unique local solution for a continuous state-Lipschitz first-order system on an open domain ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).
  | 
  | [F2] A solution of a first-order system is equivalent to a solution of the associated Volterra integral equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).
  | 
  | [F3] Every Picard-Lindelof IVP has a unique maximal solution on an open interval, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]).
  | 
  | [L1] A solution whose graph approaches a compact interior region at a finite endpoint extends past that endpoint ([[lem-ode-extension-from-a-compact-interior-region]]).
  | 
  | [L2] A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its maximum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).
  | 
  | [L3] The norm of a vector-valued integral is at most the integral of the norm ([[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]]).
  | 
  | [L4] Gronwall's integral inequality converts $u(t)\le A+\int_{t_0}^t m(s)u(s)\,ds$ into an exponential bound ([[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]).
  | 
  | 
  | 
  | **Proof technique:** direct.
  | 
  | 1.1 If $n=0$, every value lies in the singleton $M_0(\mathbb R)$, so there is exactly one map on $I$ and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous; no positive-dimensional vector IVP theorem is used. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$. Extend $C$ continuously to the open interval $(a-1,b+1)$ by setting $\widetilde C(t):=C(a)$ for $t<a$, $\widetilde C(t):=C(t)$ for $t\in I$, and $\widetilde C(t):=C(b)$ for $t>b$. Regard $M_n(\mathbb R)$ as $\mathbb R^{n^2}$. Then the right-hand side $\widetilde F(t,Y):=\widetilde C(t)Y$ is continuous on the open domain $(a-1,b+1)\times\mathbb R^{n^2}$ and is globally Lipschitz in $Y$ on every compact time interval, because $\|\widetilde C(t)(Y-Z)\|_2\le\|\widetilde C(t)\|\,\|Y-Z\|_2$. Hence [F1] gives a unique local solution through $(t_0,Y_0)$. [F1, given, construct]
  | 
  | 2.1 If $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and the prescribed value $Y(a)=Y_0$ determines exactly one map on $I$. The extension in step 1.1 has constant coefficient $C(a)$ near $a$, so its local solution is a continuation of this map; [F1] gives agreement of any two such continuations on their common interval containing $a$. This proves the singleton assertions without differentiating a singleton-domain map. For the remainder assume $a<b$. [given, F1, step 1.1]
  | 
  | 2.2 By [F3], let $J=(\alpha,\beta)$ be the maximal interval of existence of that solution in $(a-1,b+1)$. Since $C$ is continuous on compact $I$, [L2] supplies a bound $\|C(t)\|\le M$ on all of $I$. For $t\in J\cap[t_0,b]$, the Volterra equation from [F2] and the norm estimate [L3] give the forward inequality below. $$\|Y(t)\|_2\le \|Y_0\|_2 + M\int_{t_0}^{t}\|Y(s)\|_2\,ds.$$ Therefore [L4] yields $\|Y(t)\|_2\le \|Y_0\|_2 e^{M(t-t_0)}$ on $J\cap[t_0,b]$. [F2, F3, L2, L3, L4, step 1.1]
  | 
  | 2.3 For $t\in J\cap[a,t_0]$, the oriented Volterra equation gives $Y(t)=Y_0-\int_t^{t_0}C(s)Y(s)\,ds$, so [L3] gives the reflected inequality below. $$\|Y(t)\|_2\le \|Y_0\|_2 + M\int_t^{t_0}\|Y(s)\|_2\,ds.$$ The time-reflected part of [L4] therefore yields $\|Y(t)\|_2\le \|Y_0\|_2 e^{M(t_0-t)}$ on $J\cap[a,t_0]$. [F2, L2, L3, L4, step 1.1]
  | 
  | 3.1 Put $R:=\|Y_0\|_2 e^{M(b-a)}$. If $\beta\le b$, then a tail of every sequence $t_j\uparrow\beta$ in $J$ has graph points in the compact set $[a,b]\times\overline B(0,R)\subseteq(a-1,b+1)\times M_n(\mathbb R)$ by steps 2.2 and 2.3. So [L1] extends the solution past $\beta$, contradicting maximality. The same argument at the left endpoint rules out $\alpha\ge a$. Therefore $I\subseteq J$, and the restriction of the maximal solution to $I$ is defined on all of $I$. [L1, step 2.2, step 2.3]
  | 
  | 4.1 For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, step 3.1 gives existence on all of $I$. Restricting the solution on the open interval $J$ gives the domain-relative one-sided derivatives at both endpoints of $I$. Uniqueness follows from [F1] for any two solutions through the same data on their common interval $I$. Step 2.1 supplies the separate singleton case in positive dimension, and step 1.1 supplies the empty-matrix case. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎
